articles.title: Is this the future of America?
articles.summary: In this Virginia county, the infrastructure boom began two decades ago. Few residents even knew it happened, but now they’re reckoning with the next wave of data centers and what’s at stake.
articles.body: In 2007, the US was on the cusp of an economic recession, and Buddy Rizer was tasked with finding Loudoun County, Virginia, a new way to make money. Rizer’s earlier career as a radio DJ didn’t exactly make him an obvious candidate to find a solution, but he was looking for what he called a “real job” and stumbled into a role at Loudoun’s economic development authority. This new gig came with urgency thanks to the bursting of the housing bubble: More than 80 percent of the county’s revenue came from residential real estate. The goal, at the time, was to raise the commercial tax base from about 19 percent of revenue to something like 23 percent, Rizer recalls. Today, just over half of the county’s tax revenue comes from commercial sources. To jumpstart that turnaround, Rizer turned to the carcasses of another recent bubble burst — those of the dot-com era. The county had been home to the headquarters of AOL, which by 2000 was the US’s largest internet provider. Combined with its proximity to the nation’s capital and access to resources including water and electricity, Loudoun quickly emerged as the physical manifestation of the internet, the place responsible for how the majority of Americans got online. Estimates suggest that as much as 70 percent of the planet’s internet traffic passed through Loudoun County. But after the collapse of dot-com stocks in 2000, followed by AOL’s disastrous merger with Time Warner, much of that industry dried up, and Loudoun was left with hulking, empty buildings and miles of fiber optic cable already laid in the ground. Where some people saw abandoned infrastructure, Buddy Rizer saw opportunity: “And so I thought if we can fill those, that would be a good start,” he says. Rizer soon realized that the same factors that made Loudoun County attractive to AOL could once again make it a hot spot for technology. It still had an internet exchange point, lots of land, a government eager for investment, and a capable local electricity utility. “And so we came up with this plan to attract data centers.” [Image: [Image: Today, Loudoun County has another moniker: Data Center Alley. Over just a small portion of its roughly 515 square miles, it’s home to about 250 data centers, the densest concentration in the world. For a long time, residents there recall only a passing understanding of this, if they realized it at all. The development of data centers in Loudoun was just something going on in the background of many residents’ lives. They noticed construction along main roads, paid an increasingly lower property tax rate, and sent their kids to coveted public schools. The county’s data center boom arrived as tech companies expanded into the cloud, a sanitized name for the blocky buildings that house rows and rows of servers. And with that business came prosperity: 22 new schools built in just the last 15 years, tax revenue from data centers alone that exceeded the county’s operational budget by $35 million in 2024, and a decline in real property tax rate for residents from about $1.29 to 80 cents per $100 in assessed value since 2008. Some longtime residents never heard of their county’s nickname until recently, when the effects of data centers on the community started to become impossible to ignore. What had been a relatively quiet boon locally was starting to foment a national backlash elsewhere, and starting to disturb daily life in Loudoun, too. The current, massive US data center buildout has been accelerating thanks to the widespread adoption of generative AI, which has created a growing need for the physical infrastructure to run tremendous amounts of “compute” — the industry term for processing power. There are already 3,000 data centers in operation around the US, according to an April analysis by the Pew Research Center, with 1,500 more in development. When Rizer began recruiting companies to build data centers in Loudoun, he sat on conference panels for secondary markets. Now when he attends data center conferences, Loudoun is the biggest market there, and “there’s more economic developers than there are data center companies, because everybody sees the opportunity.” Loudoun County residents are also starting to take notice. Within the past few years, data centers have been elevated from an unremarkable part of daily life in Loudoun to something that many residents now think about every day. For some, it’s the constant hum they hear from their decks; for others, it’s the transmission towers that loom over their favorite green space, or the surprise call from their energy utility that one of those towers could go up in their own backyard. While residents recognize that data centers have brought a lot of prosperity to the county, they’re beginning to wonder how much more they can take. As communities around the country begin recognizing the potential opportunities of building data centers, the efforts have also faced immense pushback. Opposition to this development is shaping strange alliances across the political spectrum and has become a central issue in this year’s midterm elections. New York and Texas have begun pumping the brakes on new data center buildouts, worried about how their energy grids could support them without leaving residents stuck holding the bag if major tech players change plans. Local stories from around the country show that residents are coming out to community meetings in droves to oppose data centers. In at least one case, a violent attack on a local Indianapolis official appeared motivated by his support for data centers. And national polls show that many Americans do not want to live near them. With its long history hosting data centers, Loudoun residents have more recently taken to calling it something new: the canary in the coal mine of data center development. Want to know what the country’s future looks like? Loudoun County’s past gives a strong glimpse of it. Even in Loudoun, where the existence of data centers has been a fact of life for nearly two decades, Rizer says that in the last few years, community opposition has become more vocal. “Before then, people understood what we were doing,” he says. These days, residents seem more aware of the inconveniences. Rizer is no stranger to this kind of response to his projects, but the tone of the pushback is different. Residents have always had myriad worries: economic, environmental, and aesthetic. That part isn’t new. “I’ve done $70 billion of deals here, and the only thing in common is that somebody’s been against every single one of them,” Rizer says. “I have never seen, in my entire career, the vitriol, the hate that is associated with this.” Asked to put his radio DJ hat on to choose a soundtrack for this moment, he chuckles and says the first one that jumps into his head is Taylor Swift’s “You Need to Calm Down.” As Rizer and other officials in Loudoun field their own residents’ concerns about data centers, they’re also being flooded with calls from local officials across the country looking for their advice. Rizer is the first to admit that hosting a data center, let alone hundreds, is not the right choice for every community. He stands by the work he’s done to bring them to Loudoun, and still believes they’ve benefited the county on the whole. But data center expansion in Loudoun has recently taken on a life of its own, to the point that even Rizer no longer spends his time courting new facilities. “We don’t want more data centers here, but we want those that are here to be successful and continue to contribute to our community,” he says, diplomatically. But new facilities are coming anyway, and even Rizer, the “godfather of data centers,” is powerless to stop them. Over a series of visits to Loudoun County, I wanted to see for myself what it’s like to cross through communities surrounded by the cloud. Is the data center future that so many across the country seem to fear all it’s been built up to be? Long before it became Data Center Alley, Loudoun County was already solidifying its role as the hometown of the modern internet. In 1996, AOL decided to move its headquarters from neighboring Fairfax County to Loudoun, eventually employing more than 5,000 workers in Ashburn at its peak in 2004. Soon, the first internet exchange point, MAE-East, would make a similar move to Ashburn, making Loudoun the physical location where much of the world’s internet traffic flowed. It was further solidified as a tech juggernaut when telecom company MCI WorldCom also opened a large office in the area, which became its headquarters in 2003. The companies brought more than just jobs and a new workforce to the area. They also laid fiber underground across the county, attracting other tech firms to the area because of the convenient promise of low latency and proximity to the nation’s capital. The attention earned Loudoun nicknames like “the Silicon Valley of the East” and “Dulles Technology Corridor,” after the nearby airport. For a while, AOL and MCI’s presence made Loudoun an unlikely but bustling tech hub. Between 1990 and 2000, the county population doubled to 170,000. Early AOL employees have recounted lavish parties thrown by the company in its heyday, including “go-go-style dancers” and a sushi conveyor belt around an airplane at the nearby annex of the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum. During this time, data centers were already starting to pop up in Loudoun County, but with little fanfare. The first one arrived in 1997, and after that there was a slow drip of new data centers permitted in the area. In 2000, the local zoning administrator made a decision that would have lasting consequences later on, but made little noise at the time. Because data centers looked similar to offices, they became designated as “office parks,” meaning that they could be built on any land zoned for office space “by right” — bypassing more time-intensive regulatory review. That meant that unlike other commercial facilities like heavy machinery plants, which face more restrictions being built near populated residential areas, data centers could be built wherever offices had been allowed. [Image: Data center construction like at this location in Sterling, Virginia, is a common sight all around Loudoun County. Then the dot-com bubble burst. In early 2000, AOL announced a blockbuster merger with Time Warner for more than $160 billion. But as the first wave of internet companies suffered sharp declines, AOL’s ad revenue tanked, and the country’s largest provider of dial-up internet was soon undercut further by the rise of faster cable broadband. MCI filed for bankruptcy in 2002 after a major accounting scandal. By 2006, it was acquired by Verizon, and a year later, a much diminished AOL announced it would move its headquarters to New York. Soon after came the financial downturn that became the Great Recession. Looking for unique ways to pitch the county, Rizer, then a newly minted business development manager, saw an opportunity in the recently emptied buildings and miles of fiber still lacing Loudoun’s roads. From 2002 to 2005, no new data centers had been permitted. In the years after Rizer began courting them, only a few were permitted per year, county data shows, but growth was slow and steady. Then, in 2014, the number of data centers permitted jumped to seven. Rizer recalls feeling like the county could finally start relying less on its taxes from residents and more on commercial revenue. “We were catching up on schools and catching up on salaries for our workforce,” he says. He recalls no pushback out of the ordinary on any development project, and says that for 15 years, “everybody loved the data centers because of the difference it made in our community.” In 2018, data center permits tripled to 21 in a year, and they reached a new peak in 2022 at 25. [Image: The remains of the first AOL data center in the area are in the process of being demolished to make way for a new data center. Only those who were really paying attention seemed to notice that Loudoun was quickly becoming the data center capital of the world. Many longtime residents I spoke to sheepishly admit they hardly recognized Loudoun’s global reputation for data centers, though they perhaps passively noticed the new, blocky buildings that popped up along main roads or the tall transmission towers near their favorite running trail. Over the past 20 years, though, Loudoun residents have seen a direct impact of data centers on their lives, whether they knew it or not. Real property tax rates declined dramatically, while property values have gone up in some communities as much as 182 percent in the last decade, even at residences close to data centers, according to county officials. The county has paved smooth roads and built sprawling athletic fields, a recreation center with an Olympic-size pool, and an average of nearly one and a half state-of-the-art public school buildings every year for the past 15 years, all thanks largely to the revenue generated by the county taxes data center companies have to pay anytime they get new equipment. And while data centers have gotten a reputation for creating relatively few jobs once they’re constructed, the county says that for every job inside those buildings, three and a half non-construction jobs are “supported” throughout the rest of the state economy. Those include ongoing maintenance at data centers, like electricians or HVAC technicians, and employment at other tech companies that move to Loudoun to be near where the data lives. While the data centers take advantage of a long-standing tax exemption from the state, Rizer emphasizes that the county has never spent a dime to attract them to the area. “A majority of the people that live here now only know prosperity, only know the strongest local economy in the country, only know great services and great schools,” Rizer says. “And so they don’t necessarily connect to that. They don’t see that common thread between the fact that the data centers are here and they have a great quality of life.” [Image: Soccer fields at Hal and Berni Hanson Regional Park have been made possible through data center tax revenue. My most recent visit to Loudoun is on a July day when wildfire smoke that’s wafted down from Canada has sent air quality into a Code Purple. The ashy filter makes the grayish buildings all around look especially drab, though when I visit a local bike trail lined with trees and transmission towers, I still see plenty of cyclists braving the AQI that exceeds 200 in some spots. Julie Bolthouse, a longtime Loudoun resident who grew up across northern Virginia, drives me by the old AOL campus and points out a building with a playground on the other side of the street. “That used to be a major daycare center here in the heart of Data Center Alley, because there were so many people who worked here,” she says. “Now it’s just these big, giant computer energy-guzzling, water-guzzling warehouses.” [Image: Loudoun County officials say that tax revenue generated from data centers benefits public schools like Independence High School. The lot where the old AOL campus sat is now filled with construction equipment and several-story buildings. The old headquarters has been demolished to make way for — you guessed it — more data centers. Throughout Loudoun, Bolthouse remembers land that now houses data centers being home to business centers and dentist’s offices. She returned to the area after college, enjoying that it made an easy trip to both DC and Virginia’s Shenandoah National Park, and feeling comfortable in an area that’s generally not prone to major weather events like hurricanes. In 2017, the organization she joined, Piedmont Environmental Council (PEC), began tracking the impact of data centers on the local environment. A year later, Loudoun’s Board of Supervisors had one of its most contentious votes ever, narrowly approving a 750,000-square-foot data center spanning over 100 wooded acres near Goose Creek. Groups like PEC loudly objected to the development over environmental concerns, while those in favor of the proposal argued development would happen there regardless; it was just a matter of what would get built. [Image: Data centers have become a regular sight and part of daily life in Ashburn, Virginia. Today, Bolthouse is the director of land use at PEC and helps lead a coalition of Virginia groups that advocate for stronger protections, tracking, and transparency around data center development. Bolthouse isn’t dispositionally anti-data center, nor does she want to see existing ones in the area torn down or shut off. But she does advocate for a pause on new development. “This industry is kind of creating a narrative that they’re up against communities, and that there’s a community backlash, and we just need to explain to the communities the benefits of data centers,” she says. “But what they’re really up against is physics. They’re up against the reality of what it takes to build out gigawatts of power, and the impact of building out gigawatts of power has direct impacts on people.” Recently, she’s found, more of her neighbors are paying attention. She recalls 2025 as a turning point, where PEC no longer had to do the legwork to get people invested, but instead was triaging which press requests would make the most impact given its limited capacity. And for residents, data centers were becoming more than just eyesores. They were beginning to disrupt life in Loudoun. Vicky Hu lives in a red brick home on a cul-de-sac beside a peaceful, tree-lined stream. Her backyard stretches far along the water, where a white gazebo gives shade to sit and watch the deer she says regularly cross her yard. Including her mother and daughter, three generations of Hu’s family have lived in this house. Having grown up in the city of Taipei, Hu marveled at the nature that surrounded her new home: deer as well as turtles and cranes. “To me, this is like a dream. My dream home,” she tells me. [Image: Madison Taggart says she doesn’t want to think about what her childhood backyard would be like if forced to adopt a transmission tower. Until last year, when Hu got a call that pierced that dream. She got a voicemail from a Dominion Energy representative and first wondered if there was an issue with her energy bill payment. Instead, she was told that a new transmission line connecting two substations would cut directly through her backyard. “Are you out of your fucking mind?” she yelled at the rep. On the day I visit, the gazebo is filled with poster boards of blown-up maps of the community — and new development plans that threaten to overtake it. The trees along the stream are tagged with bright pink ribbons tied around their trunks. They mark the land Hu’s family says would be cleared should Dominion Energy’s plan to string 185-foot transmission towers through their backyard go through as planned. “It’s like the sort of thing you only think you’d see in a dystopian nightmare,” Hu’s daughter, 23-year-old Madison Taggart, tells me as she shows me around her childhood home. Growing up, Taggart says that home always felt “like a timeless place that no one else could touch.” Hu bought it shortly after her daughter was born, having seen the community built from the ground up. She worked for a developer and recalls watching workers bury power and communication lines beneath the community from her trailer across the road. By 2003, she’d nearly finished selling the community, except for one lot that was reserved for a VP at her company. As Hu’s aging mother struggled with the stairs in her townhome, she kept thinking about that lot on the cul-de-sac next to the water. She asked her colleague if she could buy it, and two years later, she moved in. Now, Hu is engaged in a yearlong fight to redirect the transmission line to another route — one that, so far, she’s on the losing end of, pending an appeal to the Supreme Court of Virginia. After that first phone call, Hu said she ran around the neighborhood “like a crazy woman,” ringing doorbells and asking if anyone had heard of the proposal. She said they hadn’t. By the time I visit, a sign in her backyard shows a diagram of the proposed 185-foot transmission tower next to a comparatively stout Statue of Liberty (if you exclude the base she stands on). Dominion insists that building the transmission line is necessary to power not only data centers, but also homes, businesses, schools, and hospitals. The local school district has been dragged into the fight over the route as well, though, with one proposal cutting close to two nearby schools. Hu’s homeowners association donated a portion of land that would be cut through to the school district, preventing it from being seized by eminent domain. Both the school district and residents in Hu’s community have been fighting the planned routes, and worry that the expansion could signal even more encroachment on key facets of the community down the road. “There’s also a deep concern for having this be a precedent that it could normalize easing the planning by just putting them on school property,” says April Chandler, Loudoun County School Board chair. Her concerns are with the kids and faculty of her community. “As a school board member, it’s not my job necessarily to consider what’s best for Dominion Energy or for data centers.” [Image: Dominion Energy’s proposed transmission tower would loom taller than the Statue of Liberty. Despite working or living in Loudoun since 2000, Hu had never heard the nickname “Data Center Alley” until last year, when a Swiss reporter came to interview her about life in the data center capital of the world. Now, she can’t unhear it. She notices transmission towers everywhere she goes. And she worries nowhere is truly safe from the ever-expanding buildout. “This is just the first power line coming through a neighborhood. Where do you think the rest of the power lines [are] going to go through?” she asks. She predicts that in the next five to 10 years, “when you look at the sky in Ashburn … you’re going to see a power line running everywhere, like a spiderweb.” Should she lose the fight to preserve her backyard, Hu says she’d have no choice but to leave. “Do I want to stay here sitting on my deck watching the power pole? … Or should I stay here for a couple years to see if I’m going to get cancer or a brain tumor?” She has lost sleep and hair fretting over how to save her home this past year. “It’s just very sad,” she says. “You‘re thinking, ‘You work your whole life, you own something.’ But you actually don’t own it, because a power company can say, ‘I like your house. I want to take it.’” As I get out of the car a couple blocks down from the Vantage VA2 data center, I can already hear the whirring. Because I visited on a day with such poor air quality, what I’m told are usually invisible emissions plumes make a faint outline in the smoggy air. They’re emitted, Bolthouse tells me, by the diesel generators powering the facility. She compares the noise to that of a lawn mower. (I later find out that the generators are never supposed to run on day with such poor air quality, but an emergency circuit issue required them to kick in temporarily.) It doesn’t always sound like a lawn mower, though. Other days, the gas turbines that power the data center make an even more annoying high-pitched squealing noise, nearby residents like Lindsay Shaw tell me. We meet while she’s out for a walk with her dog, and she describes the way the sound permeates into her home. Constant light from the data center shines right into her bedroom at night unless the bathroom door is fully closed. Her fiancé has taken to wearing an eye mask. [Image: [Image: Nobody wanted it this way. In an ideal world, Vantage would have done what hundreds of other data centers in the area have done and connected to the Dominion energy grid by the time the site went online last year. But after Vantage had already signed agreements with customers leasing space in the new data center, Dominion informed Vantage it didn’t have enough capacity to get the 800,000-square-foot data center on the grid. Rather than let the building sit dormant until Dominion built up capacity, Vantage decided to create its own energy source using gas turbines. This is becoming more and more common in other parts of the country, as the new AI-motivated data centers require vastly more energy than the old cloud servers. Residents and local politicians acknowledge that the Vantage site is an outlier because of its unusual reliance on on-site generated power from natural gas — albeit a very annoying one. Before it was built, Shaw tells me she thought a data center would be among the best options that could come to the lot across the street, in part because it wouldn’t be something that would drive a lot of traffic near what she says is an already dangerous intersection. But now she says the data center has caused plenty of other problems and feels the operators have not been proactive enough in engaging neighbors. Vantage’s senior vice president of global public policy, John Stephenson, says he “would respectfully disagree” that they haven’t proactively engaged nearby residents. He notes that they held a community meeting at a nearby brewery to field questions early on, but admits that “in retrospect, we probably could have done more.” The company has taken different approaches to mitigate the noise, including installing insulation and repositioning the turbines to lower their tone. But residents who live near other data centers throughout Loudoun — even those that don’t have to generate their own power on-site — also complain of noise. Jason Mello says he hears a constant “low-frequency drone” he attributes to the HVAC systems of nearby data centers from his Ashburn home. Living near Dulles Airport, many Ashburn residents are used to the sound of planes overhead, “but planes come and go. The data center hum never stops.” Mello shows me videos of the noise from his deck outside a town hall meeting where we meet. He says he’s already spent $2,600 getting two new window inserts, with three more to go in his bedroom. He was quoted at least $15,000 for new siding that would further mitigate the noise. “As a homeowner, if I want to live in peace at night, that addresses the inside,” he says, “but if I’m sitting on my deck, I can constantly hear that humming. And I think that’s why you got to fix the problem also at the source.” [Image: Data centers have become next-door neighbors for many Loudoun County residents. Several residents tell me that the boom in infrastructure needed to support the data centers has impacted their ability to enjoy the natural resources of Loudoun that once attracted them. “You can barely hear the birds anymore,” says Jessica Medeiros, another resident who lives across the street from the Vantage data center. Even when she tries to retreat from the noise near her home, she’s regularly reminded of the data centers’ presence. As a regular runner on the famed Washington and Old Dominion trail for the past 20 years, Medeiros says the “constant construction,” towering power lines, and reduced shade because of cleared trees “ruins the experience with nature.” She often says that when she dies, “I want my ashes scattered along the trail. But I think that trail’s going to look a lot different in another 10 years.” “The greenery is gone. The sense of community is gone. It feels very stale,” says Jenny Marza, another Loudoun County resident. “There’s no more trees left and every inch is taken up by greed.” While fighting new development near her own home, Marza has already felt pressure from the data center explosion on her small export logistics business. For years she’s been looking at buying office and warehouse space in the area to be near the airport, but prices have been so astronomical that she’s been forced to continue leasing. Now, even her current office rent has skyrocketed — she suspects because every landlord knows that data centers are willing to pay an average of $3.76 million per acre. Marza says “I’m kicking myself” over a warehouse she came close to buying last year for around $5 million, but held off because it was more space than she needed at the time. “And then we put a pause on the search for two years and when we returned, it was like, ‘Holy crap, there’s nothing left.’” Anything that was selling at $5 million was now $10 million. To Marza, the residential property tax savings and increased home values mean little when compared to the quality-of-life concerns she has and the ability to help her small business survive. “I feel like it’s a drop in the ocean of what they’re getting in return,” she says. “I feel like nobody protected our interests as a community.” “Done the right way, you can be good neighbors,” Shaw says, reflecting on the Vantage site near her home. “But this one was done like that shady neighbor next door that has people coming in and out all hours of the night. And then the FBI raids them and you’re like, ‘Well, I knew something shady was going on.’” When I arrive at the Loudoun government building on a July evening shortly before 6:30PM, I’m handed a red flyer outside by a group advocating for local government control of utilities used to power data centers. Inside, the nearly full room is prominently speckled with light blue shirts that read “I support data centers.” The shirts list the reasons: “Because I like: lower taxes, excellent schools, better job opportunities.” They also include caveats: “When they are: in the right location, well-designed, quiet, environmentally sensitive.” The slogan doesn’t exactly roll off the tongue. I comfortably score a seat, but later hear complaints from some attendees who say they arrived shortly after me and were relegated to the overflow room. Though it’s a first-come-first-served event, those critical of data centers grumble that industry supporters seem suspiciously well organized in their early arrivals. Still, it doesn’t have the kind of fireworks or soundbites that have made community meetings about data centers around the country into national news. While some residents voice strong frustration, the two-and-a-half-hour forum is cordial and respectful of Board of Supervisors Chair Phyllis Randall’s request of no cheering nor jeering. [Image: Tippett’s Hill Cemetery, one of the oldest African American cemeteries in the area, is surrounded by data centers. Randall is in a tough spot. As head of the elected nine-member panel tasked with adopting local ordinances, appropriating funds, and rezoning land, Randall has just enough power for her constituents to lay responsibility for their criticism at her feet, yet not enough to change some of the things she says she wishes she could. At the meeting, she listens to residents’ concerns, promising to follow up with phone calls for some while repeatedly acknowledging and lamenting the quality-of-life frustrations many of her neighbors have about living near data centers. But she also declines to give ground on topics she said are unfounded or detached from political reality. Randall walks residents through the history of data centers in Loudoun, including what they are and how they came to be zoned the same way as office parks. Before getting to the audience participation portion, she clicks to a slide that says “4 Things That Are Unpopular But True” with a grimace emoji. The first: At one point in time, residents actually preferred data centers over new housing developments. She references opposition to a 2021 proposal to build up to 779 residential housing units in Ashburn, called Hyde Park. Across about 125 comments, residents reportedly worried about increased traffic and infrastructure strain. Nearly two years after submitting the application, the developer withdrew and decided to establish a by-right data center there instead. “One of my worst days was January 5th, 2023, when the applicant called me and said, ‘Forget it. I’m going to go build a data center,’” Randall says. “And I pretty much begged them not to.” The second unpopular truth: It’s not legal for Loudoun to enact a moratorium on development without the state’s permission. Third: Both the Biden and Trump administrations have indicated AI infrastructure buildout will be a national priority, so that’s unlikely to change anytime soon. And fourth: Despite resident backlash to certain data center land use exceptions the board has granted, the alternative would have been that those data centers could take the land by right anyway, with much less in return. The lesson being, if data centers can break ground whether government officials want them to or not, the county might as well get something out of it. Residents who speak at the hearing do not dispute her account of the county’s history. Many express frustration about the buildings encroaching on greenery or creating annoying and near-constant noise issues. But many others, including several in the blue shirts, argue in support of data centers as stewards of the community they are proud to be known for. One Ashburn resident describes a peaceful experience living across from a data center. “When the weather is good, I’ll open my bedroom windows, from which I can see it directly. It is silent, it is clean. It is a good neighbor,” he says. Another resident, who leads the nonprofit Northern Virginia Science Center Foundation, credits data centers with generating revenue that can help fund such endeavors to a greater degree than it sees in nearby Fairfax. The organization lists Loudoun County, Dominion Energy, and data center company QTS among its partners. Randall affirms residents’ data center complaints, but also fact-checks several claims about supposed data center projects she says never existed in the first place. One Ashburn resident, for example, bemoans what he calls the “Ashburn Commons proposal” that would create a blight next to existing housing, greenery, and other community institutions. Randall asks him to clarify if he is thinking about a proposal near the Harris Teeter grocery store. “Yes!” he answers. “That’s not real,” Randall says. Her colleague adds the would-be developer hasn’t even submitted a formal application for it, and the government had denied an initial request. “Well,” the resident cries out, “praise the Lord on that!” For all the gripes, I’ve still yet to meet anyone in Loudoun County who actually says they oppose data centers entirely. Whether they’re currently living next to gas turbines or their backyard could potentially be seized to build a transmission tower, Loudoun residents still recognize that data centers help power the technology we use every day. After all, they need to go somewhere. Why not there? But even if Loudoun residents have accepted the economic benefits as a tradeoff for the loud eyesores near their homes, it doesn’t mean they’re open to an expansion of that deal. “It’s not about trying to get rid of the existing data centers. These data centers are here. They’re running. I don’t want them to go anywhere,” Bolthouse says. “The question isn’t, ‘Do we need data centers?’ The question is, ‘Is it worth threatening our air quality, threatening our water supply, and throwing our communities into chaos, and taking people’s private land for transmission lines to get it?’” I spoke with over half a dozen Loudoun residents, and universally, this is what they want communities considering data centers to understand: Know what you’re getting into. That means making sure existing laws and ordinances will apply to data centers, that local utilities have a plan to ensure enough capacity for the expected buildout, and that neither data centers nor the infrastructure needed to power them can be built too close to homes or schools. Even Rizer says the buildout in Loudoun has, in some places, gone beyond what he’d have hoped. “There’s no data centers here that aren’t where they’re allowed to be, but I think sometimes there’s a difference between what you’re allowed to do and what is probably best for the community,” he says. “And that’s what we’ve had to clean up a little bit.” At the town hall, Randall showed aerial images of several residential communities that were directly bordered by data centers. Those arrangements are not what any Loudoun official or resident considers ideal — but even so, she said, property values in those communities have only gone up. There are limits. Loudoun hasn’t had a strategic focus on bringing in more data centers since 2019, Rizer says. More recently, the local government is pursuing a plan to pump the brakes further — doing away with the ability for data centers to use office-zoned land by right, and considering pausing new permit reviews while contemplating zoning changes that could better address community impacts. When peers around the country contact him about whether they should invite data centers into their communities, Rizer says, “It’s not right for every place. So do you want them? And if you do, where do you want them? How many do you want? And under what conditions would you take them?” For Loudoun, unlike many yet-to-be-developed areas in the US, there is a definitive end in sight. The county has an ever-diminishing amount of space left to develop data centers, after which point it will continue to collect tax revenue when the companies update equipment within their walls. Loudoun residents hope that by the time it gets to that point, the things that they love about the area are still there. For many, it’s the convenience of living near DC, but still close to nature. It’s also often about the quality public schools, funded in part with the revenue raised by the colossal energy-guzzling slabs in their backyards. [Image: HVAC units on top of data centers can contribute to the loud noise many residents complain about. AOL’s roots helped make Loudoun the first major data center capital, and that came with both advantages and challenges. For communities starting to consider their first data center today, Bolthouse says they’re in a much better position than Loudoun was because the industry isn’t yet “embedded” in layers of government. She still thinks their story could become a beacon of hope for others, rather than a warning — but it’s an uphill battle to get there. “I don’t want to be the example of what not to do,” she says. “I want to be the example of what to do. I want to bring journalists out to see how we fixed problems, how we are doing much better, and how communities are happy with these facilities because they’ve done something better.” Hearing Bolthouse’s frustration with the ever-expanding energy demands imposed by data centers, it’s surprising to hear her embrace the ones that are already here. But for all the friction they’ve caused in her community recently, it’s also clear from my visits and conversations that data centers have played a central role in supporting many positive aspects of life in Loudoun. The question, now, is whether Loudoun can manage its existing demand and successfully serve community needs as the data center footprint continues to grow. If Bolthouse sounds optimistic, she is certain that something has to give. In the past, Loudoun’s data center buildout was quiet and steady. Today’s is anything but. “I don’t see how that happens with the scale and speed to market that the industry is pursuing.”

articles.title: The robot butler dream doesn’t have legs
articles.summary: Humanoid robots will be on show at IFA to show us how far they’ve come. But they’re just not ready for our homes.
articles.body: The idea of humanoid robots running our homes has been the stuff of science fiction for years. But unlike hoverboards and self-tying sneakers, a robot housekeeper has never felt close to rolling into our homes. Until now. This has been the year of the humanoid robot. At CES, there were dozens of human-shaped bots on the show floor, a handful designed for homes. US-based robotics company 1X has already put its $20,000 Neo robot into homes to do housework (with a lot of remote assistance); and this week at the IFA tech show in Berlin, around half a dozen humanoids, mostly from China, will take to a catwalk to show off the alarming (?) acceleration of their skills as they plan to backflip into our lives. [Image: Robots on the Runway takes place on Saturday, Sept. 5th at IFA in Berlin, and will include robots from Primebot Robots, Agibot, Unitree, Ollobot, and Astrall Dynamics. But do we really need mechanical, multimodal robots that do our housework, or is there a smarter path that doesn’t involve 170-pound hunks of metal that could accidentally kill your dog with one misstep? I’ve spent the last few years testing robots in my home; from robotic vacuums that can sweep and mop, to bots that mow my lawn, scoop cat poop, and cook dinner for me (all different bots, to be clear). I’ve also invited in Amazon’s Astro robot and several companion robots, including Ecovacs’ LilMilo, SwitchBot’s Kata, and Intuition Robotics’ ElliQ. During my time with these robots, two things have become clear. First, despite my tech-reviewer fascination with humanoid robots, a fully humanoid robot housekeeper isn’t practical. Unlike factories, where humanoids have seen some success, homes are messy, unpredictable environments. Also, most people have stairs. Solving that problem requires a robot that can either fly or have a pair of legs that can exert substantial force — neither of which is a good fit for a home. (Just ask Ring where its much-touted Always Home flying camera is). Second, tech history has proven that precious few gadgets do multiple things well. We don’t need an expensive jack of all trades and master of none. At CES, I walked around the Las Vegas show floor with a bottle of laundry detergent, challenging every humanoid robot I met to open it. Not a single one could. I was repeatedly told it had to learn how to do it first. [Image: Switchbot is another smart home company developing a robot housekeeper. Its Onero home robot will be at IFA this week, showing its skills. What I think is more practical is a robot brain: an AI-powered smart home controller that can orchestrate the autonomous devices we already own based on the needs of the house and its occupants. Instead of one expensive machine trying to do everything, imagine a smart home that can proactively manage itself and adjust to the occupants: send the robot vacuum out when the dog spills his kibble, start the washing machine when energy is cheap, or dispatch the lawnmower when the edges need trimming. Today, smart homes are mostly command-and-control or based on routines you create that require triggers. A robot brain could run your home autonomously and use reasoning to adapt when the home’s unpredictabilities arise. This appeared to be the idea behind Samsung’s Ballie robot (which never launched), and LG’s CLOiD humanoid (which looks more promising). It’s also the long-term vision of Amazon’s Alexa Plus and Google’s Gemini for Home smart assistants. No one is close. [Image: Doova is a robot companion designed for seniors living alone. At IFA this week, Tuya, a global AI cloud platform service provider, will launch a similar concept but with a tighter focus. Doova is an AI home companion designed to help seniors living alone. It is a short, round robot on wheels with no arms, but it does have “dynamic facial expressions.” Tuya says Doova can track its owner in the house and be ready to assist in an emergency. It can open a live video call with family if they don’t respond. It will also provide “conversational companionship” and work as a smart home hub to control lights, curtains, and kitchen and bathroom appliances. The company hasn’t announced a price or release date, but says it will come to market. Doova doesn’t need to fold laundry or load a dishwasher to be useful; it can understand what’s happening in the home, connect people to the home, and control machines already there. It does, however, present the other huge challenge for robots in our homes: They need cameras to navigate and interact, and cameras in our homes raise major privacy concerns. [Image: CLOiD loading (plastic) dishes into a dishwasher. Hands could make home robots much more useful, but they are very hard to perfect. Still, there is appeal in the idea of a robot brain that can do some manual chores — pick up clutter, load and unload a washing machine and dishwasher, and other tasks that require hands. I tested a robot vacuum with an arm that was supposed to pick up shoes and socks, and it mostly failed, but the idea is solid. The middle ground between an imposing full-sized humanoid with legs and an armless robot companion is a wheeled bot with arms. That’s the direction LG took with CLOiD, a wheeled bot/smart home controller with arms boasting 7 degrees of freedom and five individually actuated fingers per hand. I saw a live demo of CLOiD at CES this year using these appendages to perform simple tasks like folding clothes, taking items out of the fridge, and loading a washing machine, but not unscrewing a detergent bottle (I guess it uses pods?). Along with (very slow) physical actions, it also connected to and controlled smart appliances, including a washer, dryer, and oven. This week, LG announced it is training hundreds of CLOiDs at a new data factory in Seoul, where they will practice a range of cleaning tasks in a home environment. By the end of this year, the company says this training data will feed roughly 100,000 hours of training data — equivalent to 12 years — into its own robot foundation model, built using Nvidia Cosmos open-world models. It’s clear home robots are coming. But I don’t believe we need a robot butler that caters to our every need — very few people could afford one anyway. The future of home robotics isn’t one machine that can do everything, but a team of robotic machines, coordinated by a robot brain. And if that brain happens to come with a pair of hands that can open my laundry detergent, even better. [Video: Are humanoid robots the next smart home gadget?]

articles.title: Elon Musk’s heterodox robotaxi philosophy gets put to the test
articles.summary: Tesla is launching the Cybercab, the ultimate test of Elon Musk’s heterodox, stripped down, camera-only approach to autonomous driving.
articles.body: Believe it or not, the Tesla Cybercab is coming. Nearly two years after Elon Musk first unveiled the gold-tinted, gull-wing door sporting, steering wheel-free two-seaters as the future of Tesla’s autonomy efforts, the company is finally putting them into operation as part of its robotaxi service in Austin, Texas. Public rides are here, and as Musk fans will assert, the era of Tesla’s robotaxi dominance will begin. Or will it? Musk has bet his company — and his trillion-dollar pay package — on a stripped down, barebones autonomous driving system that eschews multiple sensors used by all of his rivals in favor of a camera-only approach. The Cybercab, as a purpose-built autonomous vehicle without traditional controls, embodies this bet. Musk believes he can forge his own path to robotaxi success — and the Cybercab is his gilded vehicle of choice. We’ll soon know if he’s in for a crash. The Cybercab will be using a modified version of Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (FSD). For the company’s millions of vehicle owners, FSD remains a Level 2 driver assist feature that requires human supervision. In the Cybercab, it will be monitored by remote operators who theoretically can step in if there’s a problem. FSD and Autopilot have been linked to dozens of fatalities and thousands of crashes. Using only cameras and an AI-powered neural net, the Cybercab will need to navigate a complex, unpredictable environment. Without conventional controls, there will be no human fallback in case the autonomous system fails. And after years of blaming crashes on their drivers, Tesla will now bear full legal responsibility if something goes awry. For years, Musk has coasted on brash promises for an autonomous future. With tomorrow’s Cybercab launch, those promises are going to face harsh scrutiny that’s not easily overshadowed by rows of gleaming robot cars hitting the road. [Image: [Image: Waymo’s new Ojai robotaxis (left) versus Tesla’s Cybercab (right). For over seven years, Musk has thumbed his nose at the conventional wisdom around self-driving cars — specifically that more sensors equals more safety. At Tesla’s inaugural “Autonomy Day” event for investors in 2019, he laid out his vision for a sleek, simplified autonomous driving system that avoided the protruding sensors of the Waymo cars of the time. The top target for his ire: lidar. The light beam sensor that practically everyone views as an essential ingredient for self-driving cars is “a fool’s errand,” Musk said at the event in 2019. And “anyone relying on lidar is doomed. Doomed. Expensive sensors that are unnecessary. It’s like having a whole bunch of expensive appendices... you’ll see.” The crux of his argument is that humans use their own eyes to make driving decisions, so why not autonomous vehicles? Tesla once relied on radar, in addition to cameras, as part of its perception system, only for Musk to do away with the sensor in 2022. The company’s own engineers tried to persuade Musk to keep radar. They worried that without radar, Tesla’s self-driving system would be susceptible to basic perception errors if cameras were obscured by rain or sunlight — which could lead to crashes. They were rebuffed. The reason everyone else uses lidar underscores the limitations of Musk’s camera-only approach. Cameras only provide flat, two-dimensional images, requiring Tesla to use computer vision and neural networks to approximate depth and distance. A camera-only system leaves itself vulnerable to sunlight glare, while a multi-sensor system has additional data in case its perception is blinded. And cameras struggle in adverse weather, like snow or fog, while lidar and radar can often pierce through these conditions. Few of Musk’s predictions have come true, including his condemnation of lidar. Waymo, which uses lidar in addition to cameras and radar, is operating a fleet of 4,000 fully driverless vehicles in up to 14 cities across the US. This is the largest, more fully realized deployment of self-driving cars in the US — and possibly the world. Lidar hasn’t slowed Waymo’s progress; in fact, its engineers strongly believe the sensor helps accelerate it. In a recent talk at Y Combinator’s Startup School, Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov agreed that cameras have gotten good enough to closely approximate human driving. But if the goal is to exceed humans and build a system that truly excels at safety, then cameras alone aren’t good enough. If you’re targeting full autonomy and superhuman performance, Dolgov said, “you find that weak sensing just leads to a safety curve that flattens out way too early.” But Musk claims that a camera-only system is more affordable to mass produce, and thus will enable Tesla to deploy Cybercabs more quickly than Waymo. There’s no arguing that the Cybercab is cheaper to produce than Waymo’s sensor-laden robotaxis, but the lack of lidar isn’t the only reason. Tesla’s also saving money by leaving out traditional controls like steering wheels, pedals, and mirrors. The company argues this helps create more passenger space, but the hope is that it will also make the vehicle more profitable to manufacture. "“You find that weak sensing just leads to a safety curve that flattens out way too early.”" - Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov At Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in 2024, Musk promised that people could buy the Cybercab for a price “less than $30,000.” Someone could theoretically buy a small fleet of Cybercabs to operate as a bespoke robotaxi service, he said. But to sell the Cybercab to regular people, Tesla will need an exemption from federal safety rules that require vehicles to have steering wheels and pedals. If it tries to self-certify, it may run into the same trouble that tripped up Zoox for several years. (The Amazon-owned company eventually got its exemption, with heavy conditions.) Tesla will also need a permit from the California DMV to operate fully driverless vehicles on public roads. And in order to do that, it will need to demonstrate that its vehicles can operate safely — which so far, the company has not done. What happens when a Cybercab is disabled or breaks down? Other AV operators like Waymo have procedures in place for remote operators to try to move the vehicle out of the way. And if all else fails, they dispatch crews of technicians who come out and manually drive the vehicle away. For a vehicle without steering wheel or pedals, teleoperation becomes the primary failsafe. That explains why Tesla has taken to installing Starlink connections in all its Cybercab — a convenient, if not double-dealing, solution for Musk. The Cybercab may find itself stuck in Austin while Tesla works out these technological and regulatory hurdles. The Texas capital is where Tesla’s robotaxi service features the most unsupervised vehicles. It’s where Tesla feels most confident in its driverless capabilities. There is no federal policy dictating driverless car deployments in the US. Legislation that could open the gates to more Cybercab-type vehicles has been stalled in Congress for years, with no sign of budging. That leaves Tesla to fight for permission state by state, or sometimes city by city. That’s expensive, not to mention time consuming. Tesla’s current Robotaxi business has been extraordinarily difficult to nail down. The fleet’s size and supervised-vs-unsupervised status has vacillated wildly for months. Sometimes there are dozens of robotaxis available, depending on the city, but more often less than a handful are actually doing paid passenger trips. In Tesla’s most mature market of Austin, where it has been running robotaxis since June 2025, the company has approximately 110 Model Y vehicles in operation, according to Robotaxi Tracker. With the addition of the Cybercab, we should expect those numbers to grow dramatically. But as we’ve seen in the past, just because the vehicles are on the road doesn’t mean Tesla is necessarily using them for passenger trips. [Image: If you ask Tesla, its safety record is unimpeachable. The company’s dashboard of 2 billion miles claims that Tesla vehicles that use the supervised version of Full Self-Driving are involved in 40 to 90 percent fewer crashes than manually driven vehicles. But its actions also speak louder than words. Despite marketing materials that suggest the system is more autonomous than it actually is, FSD remains just a Level 2 feature that requires constant human driver supervision. The driver, not Tesla, is legally responsible when something goes wrong. Meanwhile, fatal crashes involving FSD continue to rack up. Under a 2021 standing general order by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tesla is required to report crashes where its Level 2 driver assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was hurt, killed, or the vehicle was towed. According to Electrek, Tesla accounts for roughly 85 percent of the entire industry’s reports — nearly 4,000 crashes — thanks to its status as the automaker with the most ADAS equipped vehicles. And independent trackers like Tesla Deaths record roughly 65 fatalities involving Tesla Autopilot or FSD systems between 2013 and 2025. (There could be more; Tesla redacts most of the details in its reports to NHTSA.) Tesla likes to trumpet the good stats, while hiding the bad ones. Its vehicles enjoy some of the highest safety ratings in the country, but its autonomous driving statistics remain a black box. Unlike Waymo, Tesla hasn’t submitted its safety data to any independent group for validation. Its own AI trainers have told Reuters they don’t trust its safety stats. And the company is currently under investigation by NHTSA for how it reports these crashes. Autonomous driving is all about trust, and Tesla currently doesn’t enjoy a lot of it. A recent survey found that most people think the company is misleading its customers by using terms like “Autopilot” and “Full Self-Driving.” They also don’t think the company is doing enough to ensure its drivers follow the rules — and a quick survey of social media backs up this belief. And they don’t want it to deploy fully driverless taxis. The Cybercab is sure to scramble some of these perceptions. With its future at stake, Tesla is barrelling ahead with fully driverless vehicles. A well-managed launch will no doubt be enough key-jangling to impress investors. But the public may be harder to convince.
